issues.legal_issue: A thekedar’s status in land that was the lessor’s sir or khudkasht depends on whether the land was personally cultivated under a theka made for the thekedar’s personal cultivation, or was cultivated incidentally under a rent-collection theka.
material_facts: The disputed land was the lessors’ sir or khudkasht when the theka was granted.
The land was in the thekadars’ personal cultivation on the relevant date and when the estate vested.
On considering the theka document, the arbitrator found that the theka had been made with a view to the thekadars cultivating the land personally.
The arbitrator held the thekadars to be Sirdars; the ex-landlords claimed the land as their own.
issues.conclusion: The thekadars were rightly held to be Sirdars. Where the land was personally cultivated under a theka made for the thekedar’s personal cultivation, the thekedar was deemed a hereditary tenant under section 12(1); where cultivation was merely incidental to a rent-collection theka, section 13(2)(a) made the thekedar an asami.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, a thekedar generally ceased to have a right to hold or possess land in the estate from the date of vesting, subject to section 12 and section 13(2). Section 12(1) applied when the land was in the thekedar’s personal cultivation on the specified date and the theka was made with a view to personal cultivation, making the thekedar a hereditary tenant. If cultivation of the lessor’s sir or khudkasht was merely incidental to the thekedar’s appointment to collect rent, section 13(2)(a) applied and the thekedar became an asami. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.land_status_dispute_after_estate_vesting: The proceeding concerns competing claims to land after an estate has vested.
predicates.land_was_personally_cultivated_by_theked: The thekedar personally cultivated the land on the legally relevant date.
predicates.theka_was_made_for_personal_cultivation: The agreement granting the land was made with a view to the thekedar cultivating it personally.

issues.definition: When a post-vesting land-status dispute concerns land personally cultivated by the thekedar under an agreement made for that purpose, the thekedar has hereditary-tenant status.

issues.legal_issue: An award determining land status should not be set aside for an apparent error of law when the arbitrator’s interpretation of the theka is correct.
material_facts: The arbitrator considered the theka document and found that it was made with a view to personal cultivation by the thekadars.
The Civil Judge set aside the award and remitted it for reconsideration, but the Supreme Court considered the arbitrator’s interpretation correct.
The challenge concerned whether the award could be interfered with on the ground of an error of law apparent on its face.
issues.conclusion: The arbitrator’s award was not fit to be interfered with, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the arbitrator’s interpretation of the theka did not disclose an error of law apparent on the face of the record that justified setting aside the award. It applied the distinction between section 12(1) and section 13(2)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_land_status_award: A party challenged an award that determined competing claims to land status.
predicates.arbitrator_interpreted_theka_as_made_for: The arbitrator read the agreement as having been made for the thekedar’s personal cultivation of the land.
predicates.that_interpretation_is_supported_by_the_: The agreement supports the arbitrator’s reading that personal cultivation was its purpose.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a land-status award, if the arbitrator’s reading of the agreement as intended for personal cultivation is supported by the agreement, the award is not fit to be set aside.
